n: This psalm joins two earlier passages: verses 1–5 repeat Psalm 57:7–11, and verses 6–13 repeat Psalm 60:5–12. David’s heart is ‘fixed’ — steady and resolved — to praise God with his whole being.
He calls his instruments to wake up, and promises to wake the dawn itself with his music.
He will praise God not just in Israel but among all nations.
God’s covenant love is higher than the heavens and his faithfulness reaches the clouds.

f.w: thy mercy is great above the heavens

n: David prays that God’s glory will be honored throughout heaven and earth.
The second section begins: rescue your beloved people with your strong right hand.
God speaks from his sanctuary, claiming the land as his to distribute. Shechem (west of the Jordan) and Succoth (east of it) represent the whole territory.

f.g: A central town in the hill country of Ephraim.
A valley east of the Jordan.

n: God names Israel’s tribal regions as his own. Ephraim is his helmet (‘strength of mine head’) and Judah his royal scepter.

f.g: My scepter — the tribe of kings.

n: The enemy nations are pictured as lowly servants: Moab a washbasin, Edom a place to toss sandals — a gesture of ownership.

f.g: A basin for washing feet — a humble, menial object.
Throwing a sandal over land claimed ownership.

n: David asks who will lead him into the fortified city of Edom — probably the rock city later known as Petra or Bozrah.

f.g: A fortified city, likely Edom’s capital.

n: Only God can lead them — even though he seemed to have rejected them in a recent defeat.
Help from humans is worthless; only God can truly save.

f.w: vain is the help of man

n: The closing confidence: with God, we will act bravely, and he will trample our enemies.

f.w: Through God we shall do valiantly
